extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, journalism educators, and practicing journalists interested in writing processes
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how journalists (here, science writers) use discourse knowledge and/or audience knowledge during the newswriting process, based on protocol analysis of writers' recorded thoughts while composing articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse knowledge as decision driver
rubrics_metrics.description: Results indicated that discourse knowledge, rather than audience knowledge, motivated decision making throughout the newswriting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study finds journalists' decision making is guided by journalistic discourse conventions. This implies evaluating newswriting should consider whether writers follow discourse conventions that structure choices about content, form, emphasis, and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience knowledge (explicit) as a motivator
rubrics_metrics.description: Science writers were selected because they were hypothesized to be particularly sensitive to the needs of their audience and to rely more on audience knowledge when making decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to the hypothesis, the study found audience knowledge did not primarily motivate decision making. As an evaluative criterion, explicit appeals to or invocation of audience knowledge may be less visible in actual writing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation of audience via discourse knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists learn how to accommodate the audience by relying on discourse knowledge they obtain through their educational training, professional experience and interactions with other members of the journalistic discourse community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess accommodation not only by explicit audience-targeting but by how well the writer applies learned discourse conventions (clarity, backgrounding, lede placement, framing) acquired via training, experience, and peer interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of protocol analysis to trace cognitive processing
rubrics_metrics.description: A study used protocol analysis to trace a group of specialized journalists' cognitive processing of information; five science journalists recorded their thoughts from the time they started to write an article until the time they finished; tape recordings were transcribed and analyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a methodological criterion for studying writing processes, protocol analysis involves real-time verbal reports, transcription, and analysis. When evaluating process research, consider sampling, recording fidelity, transcription quality, and analytic transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of specialized journalists (science writers) for sensitivity to audience needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Science writers were selected because they were hypothesized to be particularly sensitive to the needs of their audience and to rely more on audience knowledge when making decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generalizing findings or designing similar studies, note the rationale for selecting specialized beats (e.g., science writing) and report recruitment/sample details (here: 5 participating journalists out of ~25 contacted at professional meetings).
